retweet.text:
At the 1976 Summer Olympics in Montreal, reporters asked East German swimming coaches why their teenage female athletes suddenly had deep baritone voices and massive, heavily muscled shoulders.

The coaches laughed. They told the press they were in Montreal to swim, not to sing.

Newspapers printed the joke and moved on. When an American swimmer pointed out the obvious, that something in the pool wasn't right, sportswriters across the United States turned on her instead.

Her name was Shirley Babashoff.

She was nineteen years old, from Fountain Valley, California, and she had spent more than half her life preparing for that pool. Since the age of eight, she had trained under coach Mark Schubert at the Mission Viejo Nadadores club, waking up in the dark to swim ten thousand meters a day before and after high school.

At the 1972 Munich Games, she had won Olympic gold at fifteen. By 1976, holding multiple national records, she arrived in Montreal as the anchor of the American women's team.

Once the races began, the East German women dismantled every expectation in the aquatic center. They won eleven of the thirteen swimming gold medals and shattered world records in nearly every event.

Shirley swam the races of her life. She broke her own American records and walked away with four silver medals, posting times that would have guaranteed gold in almost any other era.

The American press expected her to smile on the podium and graciously congratulate the swimmers who beat her.

Shirley refused to play along. She stated plainly what everyone in the building could see: her competitors had developed deep voices and physiques unlike anything ever seen in women's swimming.

She wasn't media-trained, and she didn't hide her frustration when reporters pushed leading questions. She gave blunt answers and flatly refused to fake a smile for the cameras when she felt cheated on the world stage.

At the time, the International Olympic Committee had no reliable test to detect anabolic steroids, and Cold War politics prioritized keeping up the appearance of fair play. The United States Olympic Committee offered Shirley zero public defense.

American sportswriters found it far easier to attack an outspoken nineteen-year-old than to investigate an international sports machine. Columns across the country dubbed her "Surly Shirley," branding her a bitter runner-up and an embarrassment to American sportsmanship.

On the final day of the swimming events in Montreal, Shirley stepped onto the starting blocks for the 4×100-meter freestyle relay.

Her teammates, Kim Peyton, Wendy Boglioli, and Jill Sterkel, kept the race tight. When Shirley dove in for the anchor leg, she was swimming head-to-head against Kornelia Ender, the East German star who had already claimed four gold medals.

Shirley swam her leg in 55.48 seconds. The American women hit the wall in 3:44.82, beating East Germany by less than a second to win the gold medal.

It was the only women's swimming race the East Germans lost in the entire 1976 Olympics.

Even that victory couldn't shake the label the press had pinned on her. Shirley retired shortly after Montreal at nineteen years old, remembered by much of the public simply as the swimmer who complained.

Then, in 1989, the Berlin Wall fell.

In the early 1990s, the newly unified German government opened the archives of the Stasi, East Germany's secret police. Inside those files was a classified government directive called State Plan 14.25, a state-sponsored doping program engineered to prove communist superiority through Olympic medals.

The records laid out the exact milligrams of synthetic testosterone given to teenage girls. Doctors had handed thirteen- and fourteen-year-old swimmers little blue pills in locker rooms and at training tables, telling them they were vitamins. The pills were Oral-Turinabol, a potent anabolic steroid, administered in doses higher than those given to adult male weightlifters.

In the late 1990s, the doctors, coaches, and officials behind the program were put on trial in Berlin. Former East German athletes testified in court about failing livers, heart conditions, and severe birth defects in their children, victims of their own government.

Every allegation Shirley Babashoff had made in 1976 was proven as documented fact.

Still, the International Olympic Committee never changed the official record books, and the medals were never redistributed. Shirley went home to California, where she spent more than thirty years delivering mail for the United States Postal Service.
The 1976 times still stand.

She was asked to lose gracefully to a lie, and she chose to tell the truth even when her own country called her bitter for it. Why is it so often easier for people to punish the person pointing out an obvious unfairness than to confront the system behind it?

Claude has not been trained to sabotage work. Yes, it sometimes makes mistakes, and other agents might identify them, but this isn’t sabotage.

There have been a few screenshots floating around of an outdated Fable 5 system card. For the first two days of Fable 5's launch in June, we did apply non-visible safeguards to some LLM research. This was a mistake, and we reversed it on June 10. These safeguards now clearly block the request or fall back, with a message users can see (https://t.co/s0bsvowSR8).

We did train Fable 5.2 to have LLM research capabilities at about the level of Opus 5.5, and said so at launch (https://t.co/Zuk2DqOikH). This impacts capability, but doesn’t silently sabotage work.

As far as we can tell, some reports look like what we call "overcaution" in model behavior, where Claude gets overly attached to rules it makes for itself during long-running tasks. This isn’t specific to ML research, and we see it in models without these training changes (including Opus 5.5) and in our own work too. You can ask Claude to review and remove rules it made for itself, and we're working on reducing overcaution in future models. We’re not in the practice of intentionally disrupting users’ work.

We've replied directly to a bunch of reports on here asking for session IDs but please share (run `/status`)!
